title: Perceptual dimensions of tactile surface texture: A multidimensional scaling analysis

findings.consequent: fit to perceived dissimilarities of tactile stimuli
findings.mechanism: The 3-dimensional solution is the minimum dimensionality to adequately model MDS information, providing a good fit to the data.
findings.quote: The 3-dimensional solution is the minimum dimensionality to adequately model MDS information, providing a good fit to the data (S-Stress = .10, Stress = .14, 1-R² = .89).

findings.antecedent: 4-dimensional multidimensional scaling (MDS) solution compared to 3-dimensional solution
findings.consequent: improvement in fit to perceived dissimilarities of tactile stimuli
findings.mechanism: The 4-dimensional solution produced its small improvement in 1-R2 and related measures, largely by allowing for fuller—indeed, dimensional—expression of the uniqueness of a small number of stimuli perceived as very different from the others. Given a criterion of parsimony coupled with solution equivalence, the 3-dimensional MDS solution is to be preferred over the 4-dimensional solution.

stimuli.description: 17 tactile surfaces, including wax paper, cardboard, smooth plastic, nylon scouring pad, 220-grit sandpaper, felt, velvet, woven straw, cork coaster, rubber eraser, styrofoam block, brick, glossy painted wood, dry cellulose kitchen sponge, smooth leather wallet, internal surface of pine bark, and unglazed ceramic tile.

limitations: The perceptual space examined here may be specific to the stimulus textures employed.
Further studies using different stimulus sets might demonstrate the existence of additional dimensions.

The conditions of stimulation (e.g., allowing free exploration of surfaces) are likely to be particularly important and require further research to test their effects on the dimensionality of perceived surface texture.
